note: Pillar aims, solution titles and descriptions are copied verbatim from the Plan text; line breaks normalised.

pillars.aim: Connect people in hard-to-reach areas and improve usage of broadband internet

solutions.title: Solution 1: Eliminate persistent connectivity barriers across first, middle, and last mile by bundling policy advice, de-risking, and standardizing transactions.
solutions.description: The WBG will prioritize select segments – from first-to-last mile – that face the above challenges most acutely and are currently not served by the market alone. The following underserved segments will be prioritized: • Subsea cable landings in small markets, targeting Eastern and Southern Africa, Western and Central Africa, Pacific and Caribbean Islands, the Amazon River Basin, and countries connected via the Black Sea. Collaboration with partners such as Orange is being explored to drive public-private consortium for subsea cable connections for West Africa. • Missing terrestrial cross-border links, especially those that connect landlocked countries and complementing transport infrastructure along trade corridors. WBG is exploring new links between South Sudan and Kenya, Angola and DRC, and Jordan, Iraq, and Türkiye, among others as identified through regional convening of public and private sector. • Rural and remote connectivity with technology solutions that bring costs down. Innovative licensing approaches, rural tower models, and satellite services are being explored. For example, by partnering with Microsoft and Giga (UNICEF-ITU initiative) rural connectivity, including for schools and clinics, will be advanced in specific areas. • Bundled digital and energy infrastructure, including through the use of satellites, improving infrastructure sharing, and leveraging mini- and off-grid energy solutions. M300 countries such as DRC, Mozambique, Madagascar, and Nigeria will be prioritized. Across these segments, the WBG will help reshape the enabling environment in the following ways. The WBG will support countries to address regulatory barriers so that new players can enter the market more easily and existing providers have stronger incentives to extend and upgrade their networks. This will be done by focusing on competition, market entry, and open access. Opportunities for private investment will be created by reforming licensing processes, encouraging infrastructure sharing, enhancing spectrum management, and providing rights-of-way, among other reforms. These actions help reduce transaction costs for investors and enable replication of viable connectivity models. For example, infrastructure sharing can reduce capital and operating costs by 20–65%, allowing operators to deploy more and faster. These upstream efforts on policy and regulatory reforms and lowering deployment costs will contribute to reducing costs of data plans. The WBG will deploy suitable models that de‑risk and improve the viability of investment in commercially challenging areas. These will include approaches that aggregate demand, secure in-kind commitments from governments (such as rights-of-way and idle infrastructure), enable licensing and spectrum management innovations, and use WBG guarantee platform to de-risk investments and blended finance structures that lower upfront costs and reduce project risk. For instance, to unlock financial viability for improved international connectivity, the WBG will convene public and private stakeholders in relevant regions to help identify strategic subsea cable routes and landing points, high-priority terrestrial links, anchor demand, and jointly develop mechanisms for their construction, operation and maintenance. Where local hosting and traffic are limited, making connectivity less viable, the WBG will help governments expand cloud and data infrastructure using demand-driven, financially sustainable solutions that attract investment. The WBG will work with governments and private sector investors to make transactions simpler, faster, and more predictable by agreeing on and using standardized terms and documentation for tenders and proven de-risking structures. Across the value chain, this will help tenders move faster by reducing the time governments and bidders spend negotiating and reviewing contracts as well as lowering transaction costs. Clearer and more predictable transactions could increase investor confidence and make capital more likely to flow into markets that are currently seen as risky or complex.

solutions.title: Solution 2: Unlock private capital for hard-to-finance connectivity infrastructure through a Digital Access Fund, with design options to mobilize private capital
solutions.description: Complementing the upstream efforts, the WBG is also developing a Digital Access Fund to expand financing options for difficult markets. As an IFC-anchored investment fund, it aims to bring in multilateral development banks (MDBs), development finance institutions (DFIs), philanthropies such as Gates Foundation, private sector such as Microsoft, operators, governments, and other global investors to pool financing. Two options are being considered. The decision on pursuing one or both options will be made in consultation with stakeholders. Option 1: Equity investment vehicle for early- or higher-risk connectivity projects: Under this option, the WBG will develop a flexible, long-term investment fund to support internet and connectivity projects that are close to, but not yet ready for, private sector financing. The fund would blend two types of capital: “junior” capital from IDA’s Private Sector Window, donors, and philanthropies that takes on higher risk upfront, and “senior” capital from the International Finance Corporation (IFC), development finance institutions (DFIs), and private sector investors that enter once risks are reduced. This draws on experience from models such as Zafiri – a WBG and African Development Bank (AfDB)-anchored pan-Africa fund under M300 – which raised US$300 million in the first phase from a mix of DFIs and philanthropic investors and is designed to scale to approximately US$1 billion by attracting private sector investors. Like Zafiri, the Fund could operate across multiple countries by directing capital to where the project pipeline is strongest. Option 2: Investment platform for mature assets: The WBG is also considering a platform to invest in mature assets – income-generating digital infrastructure such as fiber networks or data centers. This approach allows operators to sell and free up capital from mature assets to finance new infrastructure, while giving large investors – such as pension funds and insurers – access to stable returns. Experience from India’s Infrastructure Investment Trust (InvIT) shows this model can work at scale. Due to country-specific limits on foreign investment, currency risks, and the need to match local investor preferences, the platform would likely have to start in one country before expanding.

pillars.aim: Make devices affordable, especially for the bottom 40% and MSMEs

solutions.title: Solution 3: Reduce upstream device costs by convening manufacturers to tailor specifications, advising governments on tax reform, and investing in manufacturing capacity
solutions.description: The WBG will help countries address cost drivers at the manufacturing stage and in the trade process. The manufacturing process, including cost of components, accounts for 70% of device costs, making it the single greatest determinant of what consumers pay. Uniform taxation on phone imports also keeps device prices high. South Africa’s decision to remove a 9% luxury tax on entry-level devices led to a 16% rise in first-time smartphone buyers, demonstrating that progress is achievable across diverse market contexts. To address these challenges, the WBG will engage with original equipment manufacturers (OEMs) and operating system (OS) developers such as Google and Dixon, to promote affordable, fit-for-purpose devices for first time users. The WBG will collate lessons on what works to scale local manufacturing and assembly, with the intention of identifying and adapting models that may work in Africa. In parallel, the WBG will also scale underused manufacturing capacity, for example in India, to help lower production costs. Furthermore, the WBG will support governments to address taxes and tariffs that keep entry level phones out of reach – especially in Africa – by identifying successful reforms (e.g., in India and South Africa) that clearly increased device adoption. Ongoing partnership with GSMA on device specifications and targeted tax reform will enable scaling of this solution.

solutions.title: Solution 4: Expand device penetration for low-income users and MSMEs through innovations that de-risk consumer financing and ensure right policies
solutions.description: The WBG will de-risk and expand access to capital for the retail and distribution of low-cost devices. Even when manufacturing and import costs are contained, many low‑income households and micro‑enterprises still cannot manage a one‑time device purchase. Limited credit histories and high-risk profiles constrain access to financing, and very low incomes mean that some user segments will remain unable to afford a handset even with credit. Evidence from pay-as-you-go (PayGo), buy-now-pay-later (BNPL), and operator-anchored device financing models implemented in low- and middle-income countries (LMICs) shows these approaches can expand reach to first-time users. IFC’s collaboration with Vodafone offers a replicable model for how de-risked financing can lower costs for end users. Reaching first-time users requires solutions from both public and private sectors, including joint solutions where relevant. The WBG will support governments in developing frameworks and regulations to enable and improve PayGo and BNPL models. The WBG will develop a Device Catalyst Program (DCP) to support device uptake and accelerate 2G-to-4G phone migration by working with key actors including mobile network operators (MNOs), OEMs, distributors, and governments. This includes partnerships with Google, Gates Foundation and other DFIs. The program will aggregate PayGo loans, so that risks are assessed and spread across many borrowers, and mobilize private capital to scale consumer lending to underserved segments. Private financing will be advanced through initial partnerships with Nokia, Samsung, Vodafone, and MTN. The program builds on and complements country-level interventions to deepen the consumer lending landscape. In parallel, the WBG will deliver targeted, time-bound subsidies for individuals who would otherwise be unable to afford a device.

solutions.title: Solution 5: Increase the supply of high-quality devices by unlocking regulation to formalize refurbishing and enable efficient cross-border movement of used devices, alongside targeted investment in quality-assured refurbishing companies
solutions.description: The WBG will support efforts to expand the availability of safe, high-quality refurbished devices to increase the pool of affordable options. High-quality refurbished phones can meet a growing share of device demand, especially among Micro, Small, and Medium Enterprises (MSMEs) that rely on higher-end devices for payment processing and transaction tools. Refurbished phones cost on average 25% less than new devices and the global refurbishment market is forecast to reach $100 billion by 2031, reflecting growing consumer demand and confidence. IFC’s investment in Getmobil, a Türkiye-based refurbishment platform, resulted in over 32,000 dealers across its network reporting a 60% increase in revenue from certified device sales. Strengthening and expanding the refurbishing ecosystem requires clear roles for both governments and the private sector, with the WBG supporting each in targeted ways. The WBG will help governments recognize refurbishing as a regulated domestic activity, addressing regulatory bottlenecks for cross-border trade of used devices, and developing standards (with ITU and Samsung) for refurbishment such as to ensure secure data wiping and protect the privacy of previous owners. The WBG can also engage OEMs like Samsung on scaling existing trade-in programs to increase the volume and quality of devices entering the refurbishment pipeline. Finally, WBG will invest in refurbishment companies that can aggregate idle devices from developed markets, refurbish them to consistent standards, and distribute and export them where the need is most. For example, WBG is partnering with Flipkart and Cashify in India to explore how refurbishing capacity can be scaled beyond India.

pillars.aim: Expand digitally enabled public and private services across sectors

solutions.title: Solution 6: Scale and enhance digital service delivery across sectors by leveraging the foundation of Digital Public Infrastructure and enabling reforms for interoperability and open network standards
solutions.description: The WBG will help countries design, integrate, and deliver services at scale through three interconnected interventions that build on each other. • Digital Public Infrastructure (DPI): Core digital building blocks – Digital ID, eSignatures, Digital Payments, Data Sharing, Base Registries and Verifiable Credentials – form the reusable, interoperable foundations of DPI. Evidence from leading digital economies confirms that DPI-based and open, whole-of-government architecture preserves individual data control, countries’ digital sovereignty, support competitive local markets, and avoid costly long-term dependency on a single vendor that is often difficult to reverse. This is demonstrated through India’s Aadhaar ID that reduced bank onboarding costs from $23 to $0.10, and the Philippines’s use of its national ID to authenticate 18 million social protection beneficiaries. The WBG will help countries design and implement open, interoperable DPI by providing technical blueprints, reference architecture, and policy guidance to ensure digital building blocks are built to scale and serve all sectors. The WBG will also support countries adopt the Open Network Protocol that enables DPI implementation by moving away from isolated platforms toward a shared, network model, allowing any participant to interact with others regardless of the underlying technology. By forming an Open Network Alliance with partners such as Network for Humanity, Co-Develop, Google, and MasterCard and subsequent expansion to include others, the WBG will help level the playing field and provide a unified model for public and private service providers to connect to for sectoral service delivery (see Annex 1). • Integrated Service Delivery and Life Events-Based Service Design: Building on DPI, integrated service delivery helps governments coordinate across ministries and organize services around key life events, such as having a child or starting a business. This replaces fragmented systems with seamless, end-to-end services designed around users’ experience rather than administrative structures. For example, Estonia cut citizen contact with state officials by 88%, Ireland redesigned and digitally transformed 87% of its public services, and Singapore’s LifeSG proactively matches citizens to over 100 government services. The WBG will support governments to build the institutional capacity and cross-ministry coordination needed to redesign and deliver integrated services, drawing on proven methodologies for user journey mapping and workflow redesign, including advising on technology and system design choices. • AI and Emerging Technologies in Service Delivery: Going further, AI and emerging technologies make services faster, cheaper, and more proactive once the data infrastructure and governance frameworks are in place. AI agents, geospatial tools, and digital twins can deliver personalized services at scale while keeping individuals in control of their own data and economic choices. When built on open and safe DPI, Generative and Agentic AI allow for personalized, and proactive service delivery by tailoring support to each user’s situation without requiring them to give up control over their own data and decisions. The WBG will support countries to adopt these technologies responsibly into service delivery by helping establish AI governance frameworks and investing in the institutional capacity needed to deploy and manage them effectively. The interventions above are only as strong as the partnership that delivers them. Governments lead by establishing the legal and regulatory frameworks, bringing ministries to work together, and committing to redesign services around citizen needs. The private sector contributes what governments structurally cannot – commercial innovation and the technical agility to build, operate, and continuously improve digital services at speed and scale (supported through Solution 7). The WBG will first help governments to build legal and regulatory frameworks for interoperability, including for cross-border data flows, data sharing and governance, and risk-based governance of AI and emerging technologies. With that foundation set, the WBG will provide technical blueprints and reference architecture for systems development and integration, alongside capacity building through WBG Academies and peer learning exchanges. It will help design Public-Private Partnerships (PPP) where private operators would provide these services at speed and scale under contract with government. To bring comfort to the private investors and lower the risk perception, the WBG will deploy guarantee instruments, taking advantage of well-proven structures used in other infrastructure sectors, such as transport and energy where PPP arrangements are very common. Finally, to ensure that this transformation reaches everyone, the WBG will invest in assisted service delivery channels – including community centers and kiosks – so that rural, elderly, and low-literacy users are not left behind.

solutions.title: Solution 7: Catalyze local digital industries by investing in public foundation and promoting government outsourcing for demand stimulation, and de-risking private investments to enable firms to scale
solutions.description: The WBG will help countries build more competitive, self-sustaining local digital industries by focusing on the following three interventions: • Demand and revenue stimulation for local firms: The WBG will help governments shift from state-dominated service delivery to competitive outsourcing, opening public contracts to domestic digital and AI firms. The objective is to create meaningful market opportunities and credibility for domestic firms to attract further private investment. Support for governments will include defining clear outsourcing policies and enabling a government contracting culture built around outcome-based, service-oriented, and challenge-driven models. UK’s Small Business Research Initiative has shown that government contracts can serve as springboards for private investment, and Kenya’s Government Digital Service framework has enabled local tech firms to compete for public contracts and expand into regional markets, serving as scalable and replicable models for other countries. • Viability and governance of tech valleys, parks, and special economic zones to strengthen supply: Where appropriate, the WBG will support the development of well-governed tech zones that give firms access to reliable power and connectivity, cloud resources, and structured incubation and acceleration programs. Drawing on models from Uzbekistan’s IT Park, India’s IT hubs, and Morocco’s Technopark, the WBG will adapt proven approaches for countries at similar stages of development. These are not passive real estate efforts. With the right governance, they help build local digital workforce and attract investment by projecting resource and regulatory certainty. • Local firms’ ability to scale sustainably and pursue viable exit strategies: To build a sequenced financing ecosystem that de-risks investment and enables firms to scale, the WBG will combine innovation funds and matching grants with investor mobilization, and explore credible exit pathways. In Armenia, a similar approach grew the IT sector’s contribution to GDP from 1.5% to 5.2%, created 7,600 jobs in IT and IT-enabled services. The WBG will also support the development of local and regional exchange mechanisms that allow early investors to exit and later investors to enter, drawing on models like India’s NSE Emerge that has enabled over 700 Small and Medium Enterprises (SMEs) to list with reduced compliance requirements and West Africa’s BRVM that has shown that regional exchanges can pool liquidity across countries where national exchanges are not viable. To enable all of this, governments need to create the market conditions, and the private sector needs to respond by innovating, investing, and scaling to international markets. The WBG will help governments establish the policy foundations for trusted digital markets, including digital laws, intellectual property protections, government outsourcing policies as well as regulatory frameworks to govern market mechanisms such as local or regional exchanges. Additionally, the WBG will provide governments technical assistance on the design, incentive structures, and governance models needed for tech zones. For the private sector, the WBG will provide early and growth stage financing through appropriate funding programs, cost-sharing grants, and venture funds, playing a catalytic role in attracting angel investors and local venture capital to crowd in private financing. Throughout, the Digital and AI VPU will coordinate closely with FCI and MIGA to align advisory, investment, and guarantee support.

solutions.title: Solution 8: Boost and diffuse digital skills from digital literacy to sector-specific digital and job-relevant skills through targeted technical assistance, peer-to-peer learning and public-private delivery models
solutions.description: The WBG will invest across the full spectrum of digital skilling, upskilling and reskilling, in full alignment with the WBG Education and Skills Strategy, focusing on three types of digital skills: • Digital literacy: The WBG will support two complementary elements. The first is basic digital literacy that enables people to access, navigate, and use the internet safely and confidently. The WBG will work with governments to embed digital literacy into primary and secondary education, adult literacy initiatives, combined with social protection programs, and initiatives for the aging population. This will include linking device subsidies with digital upskilling at community Wi-Fi hubs to ensure access and digital skills arrive together. The second is productivity-focused digital skills and tools, wherein the WBG will help businesses and freelancers adopt digital platforms, reach customers, and increase earnings. Together, these efforts help expand participation in the digital economy, especially among women, rural communities, youth, and persons with disabilities. • Digital skills in priority job-growth sectors: The WBG will equip workers in agriculture, health, tourism, infrastructure, and manufacturing with the specific digital skills needed to advance those industries. The WBG will support governments in designing and institutionalizing sector-specific skills pathways through local TVET institutions and universities. The WBG’s Skilling Up Lebanon program serves as a replicable model of a private sector-led digital skills initiative that trained youth in high-demand fields such as UI/UX design, DevOps, and digital marketing, delivering an 18% increase in employment and a 94% gain in earnings. • Job-relevant specialized digital skills: The WBG will increase the supply of professionals in cloud computing, cybersecurity, data, AI, and DevOps to meet growing domestic and offshore demand. The WBG will especially target young people and jobseekers by working with the private sector and academia to finance modular training supported by global industry certifications and train-the-trainer interventions. In addition, support will be provided to facilitate employer partnerships for internships – creating a pipeline of job-ready talent with stronger employment outcomes in digital and AI-related roles. In Kosovo, WBG-supported short-course digital training reduced participant unemployment from 37.4% to 30.6%. Delivering on the above requires connecting policy, delivery, and demand. Governments will set the direction and create demand – embedding digital skills into national education systems, adopting sector-specific competency frameworks, and creating the recognition mechanisms that translate digital certifications into real jobs. The private sector brings to the table elements – industry-relevant curricula, employer partnerships, and the global certification standards – that make skills more relevant for job creation and transformation. The WBG will broker public-private partnerships that serve as scalable delivery models to ensure digital skills reach those who need them most. WBG partnerships in the space such as with Coursera will help scale delivery.

pillars.aim: Adopt, adapt and advance AI solutions, and leverage Small AI

solutions.title: Solution 9: Enable locally relevant Small AI solutions by investing in replication of proven use cases, strengthening AI capacity, and cultivating an AI policy and regulatory environment
solutions.description: To ensure that AI advances development, the WBG will focus on enabling the private sector to pilot and scale small AI solutions. Small AI are practical, affordable, and locally relevant applications designed for resource-constrained settings. These solutions – which can be predictive, generative, or agentic – leverage smaller models and local datasets to run on everyday devices or edge servers, operate with intermittent or no connectivity, and reach users through familiar channels such as text messaging and voice. Small AI delivers the best-value solution as it is significantly cheaper to deploy and sustain. This approach is inherently sector and country-led: solutions are identified based on measurable demand and impact, adapted to local constraints, and implemented in partnership with governments, civil society, the private sector, and WBG regional and sector teams. Small AI solution pilots, supported by the WBG, are demonstrating early positive results. A tutoring tool in Nigeria produced two years of learning gains in six weeks. In Malawi, AI-enabled fetal monitoring contributed to an 82% drop in stillbirths and neonatal deaths. Though results are preliminary, they indicate that Small AI can deliver impact under real infrastructure constraints. Three complementary WBG efforts that span global and country level activities are at the core of advancing small AI in priority countries through close collaboration with local universities, research institutions, and local innovators and MSMEs: • Scale and replicate proven Small AI use cases: The WBG, together with other MDBs and partners, will curate a repository of practical and proven examples of Small AI addressing real-world development challenges. Based on country demand, the WBG will identify a limited number of open-source solutions and turn them into replication-ready blueprints with business models and technical guidance. These will be deployed in countries on demand including through flagship sectoral initiatives such as AgriConnect and UHC1.5. Lessons learned will be continuously captured and fed back into the repository, strengthening it as a global public good. • Strengthen AI capacity through AI and Digital Trust Academies for Governments: The WBG will establish targeted training programs for mid- to senior-level officials, including digital and ICT leaders, regulators, and sector ministry counterparts. Delivered in a hybrid format and guided by WBG and industry experts, the Academies will drive better policy, procurement, and investment decisions through practical learning, peer exchange, and South-South collaboration. It will enable public officials to support safe deployment and operation of AI as well as specialized academies on related topics on Small AI, data centers and AI computing, and cyber , data and AI. • Bring edge computing to rural and underserved communities: The WBG will pilot Small AI in a Suitcase as a mechanism to facilitate access for local AI entrepreneurs to compute and technical training to enable private sector-led adaptation and deployment of Small AI solutions in low-resource settings. This approach will focus on advancing practical locally adapted AI solutions in sectors such as education, health, and agriculture. This approach will also – where feasible – support FCV settings and small states to advance crisis response, such as early-warning systems, damage assessment, crisis mapping, and displacement monitoring, using tools that work with limited or no internet connectivity. These deployments will help countries better understand local demand for computing power and data to inform future investments. This pilot is being developed with private technology partners, such as Nvidia to support bringing edge compute capabilities to countries, and academic institutions and will be rolled out in 10 countries across regions, starting with Africa. The WBG will partner with private sector players such as Wadhwani AI Global to identify scalable Small AI use cases across sectors such as agriculture, health, education, tourism and more, and enable deployment in countries. Furthermore, the WBG will scope the AI ecosystem in countries to identify and scale startups building scalable Small AI solutions.

solutions.title: Solution 10: Strengthen AI infrastructure to establish fit-for-purpose compute capacity and AI-ready data systems by providing technical assistance for governance, de-risking private investment, and investing in public data collection and public-private data sharing platform
solutions.description: Scaling the benefits of large-scale AI requires strong foundations. The previous pillars lay critical groundwork by strengthening connectivity (Pillar 1), expanding access to affordable AI-capable devices (Pillar 2), and building specialized technical talent (Pillar 3). This solution focuses on the remaining foundations – AI compute requirements and high-quality AI-ready data and its governance. Solution 1 will strengthen appropriate compute infrastructure needed based on a country’s AI demand, as assessed by use cases under Solution 10. Evidence shows that strengthening these foundations is crucial in ensuring long-term AI development in countries and responsible and trusted AI use. The WBG will also support clear, risk-based regulatory frameworks and governance instruments for data protection, cybersecurity, and responsible AI – designed to provide certainty for investors and innovators while protecting people and markets (as explained in Section III). The approach is replicable across countries since most LICs and LMICs have limited access to affordable compute capacity, reliable datasets and regulatory frameworks and institutional foundations to deploy AI safely. For instance, less than 1% of global data center capacity is in LICs, and fewer than 20% of LMICs have modern data centers or cloud infrastructure. • Fit-for-purpose AI compute: The WBG will support countries in assessing the need and accessing fit-for-purpose AI compute capacity. Depending on country context, options may range from cloud-based AI services and distributed compute for latency-sensitive applications, to regional shared infrastructure or sovereign national compute (where justified by sustained market demand and economic and infrastructure viability). To ensure investments are right-sized, the WBG will work with governments to map and aggregate regional demand, aligning private investment with projected needs. Under Solution 1, the WBG will catalyze private investment in underserved markets by de-risking early entrants, crowding in capital, and prioritizing renewable energy. Throughout, the WBG will strengthen policy, procurement, and institutional capacity to ensure choices remain demand-driven and fiscally sustainable. Al investments in compute infrastructure will follow applicable WBG policies and standards for environment and social, climate co-benefits, and Paris alignment, and procurement. • Improved data systems for safe use of public data for AI: The WBG will foster availability of AI-ready data; support will span the data lifecycle – from collecting and checking data, to storing it securely, labelling and classifying it, managing who can access it, and ensuring accountability. The goal is to make high-value public and private data usable for AI without putting sensitive information at risk. To achieve this, the WBG will take a two-pronged approach. First, it will help governments establish robust data governance frameworks aligned with emerging AI and data protection norms (see details in Section III), invest in national data management systems to improve data cataloging and metadata, and promote open data to expand access to high-value datasets. This includes providing technical assistance and financing to create data sandboxes that give researchers, startups, and public agencies access to anonymized or synthetic data for training AI models in a controlled environment. AI-enabled government service delivery will further build on this foundation, as detailed in Solution 6. Second, the WBG will encourage the private sector to share non-sensitive proprietary data for public benefit, enabling sector-specific data libraries in areas such as agriculture and healthcare. To sustain private sector participation, data-sharing mechanisms will incorporate appropriate incentives and safeguards, including anonymization standards, trusted intermediaries, and revenue-sharing or value-exchange models where appropriate. Collectively, the Pillar 4 approach combines long-term investments in AI foundations with near-term impact delivered through scalable Small AI solutions that are trusted and locally relevant. The WBG will start with these priority areas and continue to learn, refine, scale, and expand its AI offering over time to remain effective and responsive to country needs. This dual-track approach – market-seeding through Small AI and disciplined investment in foundational enablers – positions the WBG to catalyze both immediate development impact and long-term private sector–led AI ecosystems.

cross_cutting.name: Trust, Safety, and Security
cross_cutting.description: Trust is not a feature of digitalization – it is its precondition. Connectivity without cybersecurity and data protection creates vulnerability at scale. DPI deployed without privacy and security architecture creates liabilities that grow with adoption. AI systems built on inadequately governed data erode the public confidence they depend on. Every solution in this plan generates and uses data, creates cybersecurity exposures, and depends on the trust of citizens, investors, and governments to deliver results. Digital trust is therefore the cross-cutting condition that determines whether all other investments hold. The WBG addresses this through the proposed Digital Trust Center of Excellence (DTCE), an integrated function combining cybersecurity and data protection under a unified mandate. The DTCE will work on two fronts simultaneously – helping countries build stronger digital trust systems, and raising WBG’s own standards for how it designs, finances, and supervises digital and AI operations. And put in place a screening framework to assess cybersecurity risks of IDA/IBRD operations, and as needed strengthening IFC’s due diligence efforts. Its work spans across interconnected dimensions of data collection, sovereignty, transfer, and use, and is organized as below. Foundations establishes the legal and regulatory baseline: data protection laws meeting international standards; cybersecurity laws with clear institutional mandates; and frameworks governing how data is collected lawfully and minimally, how sovereignty over nationally generated data is asserted and protected, how cross-border data transfers are governed through legal mechanisms that protect individuals while enabling legitimate digital trade, and how data use – including for AI training – is bounded by accountability, purpose limitation, and audit obligations. These frameworks are developed through legal gap analysis, model law advisory, and regulatory design support that addresses all four dimensions coherently rather than in isolation. They are anchored in budget support as DPO prior actions and as binding prerequisites for DPI deployment, ensuring legal architecture precedes – not follows – digital infrastructure. Capabilities translates frameworks into practice: strengthening Data Protection Authorities, national CERTs, and cybersecurity institutions to enforce data collection standards, assert sovereignty claims, administer transfer frameworks, and oversee data use in AI and automated systems; supporting businesses on cyber hygiene, responsible data handling, and compliance with transfer and use obligations; and embedding digital safety, data rights awareness, and individuals’ rights over how their data is collected, where it flows, and how it is used across all digital skills programs to ensure online safety. Where institutional infrastructure requires capital investment – CERT facilities, DPA offices, security operations centers, and the national data infrastructure needed to operationalize sovereignty and transfer frameworks – dedicated financing provides the physical and technical foundation. Resilience prepares countries for the incidents that will occur despite best prevention efforts – including not only cyberattacks but unlawful data transfers, sovereignty violations, and large-scale data misuse that undermine public trust in digital systems. Cyber preparedness measures and activation triggers are embedded within Contingent Emergency Response Components and Programs, providing pre-approved tools, clear escalation thresholds, and streamlined safeguards for rapid, policy-compliant response to major cyber and data governance crises. Throughout all three stages, the DTCE coordinates with peer MDBs to share diagnostics, extend delivery reach, and advocate collectively in international forums for data sovereignty, transfer, and use frameworks that reflect developing economy realities, while remaining aligned with robust international standards on cybersecurity, data protection and interoperability.
